title: Translation and Interpreting Basics
summary: Learn how translation and interpreting work: meaning and equivalence, a professional translation process, CAT tools and machine translation with costing, modes of interpreting, ethics and building a career.
audience: Bilingual and multilingual learners, language students and aspiring translators and interpreters

body.p: Translation transfers written meaning from one language (the source) into another (the target). Interpreting does the same for spoken or signed language in real time. Both are essential in multilingual countries and in international business, health, law, media and diplomacy. Africa alone has well over a thousand languages, and many people live and work in several of them every day.

list: Excellent command of the target language, usually their first or strongest language.
Deep understanding of the source language, including idioms and cultural references.
Knowledge of the subject: legal, medical, technical or literary.
Research skills and attention to detail.
Cultural awareness and judgement.

body.p: Being bilingual is a starting point, not the whole skill. Translation requires training and practice in transferring meaning accurately and naturally.

body.tip: Translate into your strongest language; most professional translators work in that direction because it produces natural, accurate text.

body.p: Languages divide the world differently, so word-for-word translation often fails. Translators aim for equivalence of meaning, function and effect.

list: Idioms: the English "It's raining cats and dogs" becomes the French "Il pleut des cordes" (literally, "it's raining ropes"); a literal translation would confuse readers.
Grammar: some languages mark gender, formality or tense differently. French distinguishes formal "vous" from informal "tu"; Swahili uses noun classes.
Culture-specific items: foods, customs, titles and institutions may have no direct equivalent; translators may borrow, explain or substitute.
Register and tone: a legal contract, a children's book and a social-media post need very different styles.
False friends: words that look similar but differ in meaning, such as the French "actuellement", meaning "currently", not "actually".

body.p: Literal (formal) translation stays close to the source structure, useful for legal texts; free (dynamic) translation prioritises natural effect, useful for marketing and literature. Most work balances both.

body.tip: After translating, read the target text alone. If it sounds like a translation, revise until it sounds natural.

body.p: Professional translation follows a disciplined process.

steps: Understand the brief: purpose, audience, deadline, format and any style guide or glossary.
Read the whole source text first, noting difficult terms and references.
Research terminology using reliable dictionaries, glossaries and subject sources.
Draft the translation, focusing on meaning.
Revise against the source for accuracy and completeness, checking numbers, names and dates.
Edit the target text alone for flow and style.
Proofread the final version, ideally after a break, or have a second linguist review it.

body.p: Translators often produce around 2000 to 3000 words of finished translation a day, depending on difficulty. A 10 000-word report at 2500 words a day needs about 4 working days, plus time for review. Agree realistic deadlines before accepting work.

body.tip: Keep a personal glossary of terms for each client; consistency builds trust and saves time.

body.p: Modern translators use technology heavily, while staying responsible for the result.

list: Computer-assisted translation (CAT) tools split texts into segments and store translations in a translation memory, so repeated sentences need not be retranslated.
Termbases keep approved terminology consistent.
Machine translation (MT) and AI tools produce fast drafts; quality varies by language pair and subject, and is often weaker for many African languages with less training data.
Post-editing means correcting machine output to the required quality.

body.p: Translators often charge per word. 2500 words at R0.80 a word is R2000. Clients sometimes pay less for repeated or matched segments: if 40% of a 10 000-word job (4000 words) is new at R0.80 and 60% (6000 words) is matched and charged at 60% of the rate, the fee is 4000 x 0.80 + 6000 x 0.80 x 0.6 = R6080.
Never paste confidential documents into public online tools without the client's permission; data may be stored or reused.

body.tip: Use machine translation as a draft only, and check every sentence; it can be fluent and wrong at the same time.

body.p: Interpreters work in real time, so they need excellent listening, memory, speaking and composure.

list: Consecutive interpreting: the speaker pauses and the interpreter renders each section, often using notes; common in meetings, courts and health consultations.

Simultaneous interpreting: the interpreter speaks while listening, usually from a booth with headphones, at conferences; it is so demanding that interpreters work in pairs and swap about every 20 to 30 minutes.
Whispered interpreting (chuchotage): simultaneous interpreting quietly for one or two listeners.
Sight translation: reading a written document aloud in another language.
Sign language interpreting: between spoken and signed languages, such as South African Sign Language or Kenyan Sign Language.

body.p: In clinics, police stations, courts and schools, interpreting errors can harm people's health, rights and safety. Untrained family members, especially children, should not be relied on for important conversations.

body.tip: Interpreters speak in the first person ("I have pain in my chest"), not "she says she has pain", so the conversation stays direct.

body.p: Professional associations publish codes of conduct. Core principles include:

list: Accuracy and completeness: do not add, omit or change meaning.
Confidentiality: keep client information private.
Impartiality: interpreters do not take sides or give personal advice.
Competence: accept only work you can do well, in subjects and language pairs you know.
Transparency: report errors or limitations honestly.

body.p: Translators and interpreters work freelance, for agencies, governments, international organisations, publishers and companies. Some documents need certified or sworn translations by accredited translators. Professional bodies, such as the South African Translators' Institute and national translators' associations elsewhere, offer accreditation, training and directories. Specialising in a field such as medical, legal or technical translation, or in high-demand African language pairs, increases opportunities.

body.tip: Build a portfolio of sample translations (using texts you have permission to use) and ask clients for testimonials.

quiz.q: Interpreting differs from translation because it deals with:
options: Spoken or signed language in real time

quiz.q: "It's raining cats and dogs" in French is best rendered as:
options: Il pleut des chats et des chiens

quiz.q: The first step in the translation process is to:
At 2500 words a day, a 10 000-word report needs about:
2500 words at R0.80 per word cost:
What does a translation memory store?
options: Previous translations of segments for reuse

quiz.q: Why must machine translation be checked?
options: It can be fluent and wrong

quiz.q: Interpreting at a conference from a booth while the speaker continues is:
Why do simultaneous interpreters work in pairs?
options: It is required for sign language only
To translate two languages at once
The work is so demanding they swap regularly
